lead: A nozzle, a duct, a throttling valve and a compressor all pass fluid steadily, so each obeys the steady-flow energy equation of 1.6. In each device one trade is left: enthalpy against kinetic energy in a nozzle, against shaft work in a compressor or turbine, and nothing gained in a throttling valve. This chapter writes those reduced forms, works out the work of compressing and expanding a gas, and shows why a fast gas in a duct behaves unlike water in a pipe.
prereq: You need: the steady-flow energy equation (1.6) and Cp, γ of an ideal gas (1.7).

blocks.text: Per kilogram passing a steady device, with c the speed, q the heat added and ws the shaft work done by the fluid:
h₁ + c₁²/2 + gz₁ + q = h₂ + c₂²/2 + gz₂ + w<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: h in kJ/kg; c in m/s; z in m; g = 9.81 m/s². c²/2 is in J/kg: divide it by 1000 before adding it to h in kJ/kg.

blocks.text: A throttling valve drops the pressure with no work and no heat, so h₁ = h₂. An ideal gas keeps its temperature; a real gas usually cools a little (the Joule–Thomson effect), which is how a refrigerator's expansion valve works. The lost pressure buys nothing: throttling is fully irreversible.

A nozzle speeds the fluid up; a diffuser slows it down. With no shaft, no heat and no height change, the quantity h + c²/2, called the stagnation enthalpy h₀, stays constant. Whatever kinetic energy the fluid gains comes out of its own enthalpy, so in a nozzle the gas cools and its pressure falls; in a diffuser it warms and its pressure rises. A jet engine slows its intake air in a diffuser for this reason.

sections.h3: Compression and expansion of a gas

blocks.text: For a reversible steady-flow process with kinetic and potential terms neglected, the shaft work put into the fluid is win = ∫v dP from P₁ to P₂: the area to the left of the path on a P–v plot, not the area under it, which is the closed-system ∫P dv. For an ideal gas (R per kilogram, T in K) the three standard paths give:

isothermal:   w<sub>in</sub> = RT₁ ln(P₂/P₁)
polytropic (Pvⁿ = constant):   w<sub>in</sub> = [n/(n − 1)] RT₁ [(P₂/P₁)<sup>(n−1)/n</sup> − 1]
isentropic (n = γ):   w<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>p</sub> T₁ [(P₂/P₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup> − 1] = c<sub>p</sub> (T₂s − T₁)
blocks.where: w<sub>in</sub> is work into the gas per kg; R = 8.314/M kJ/(kg·K), 0.287 for air; T₂s is the isentropic exit temperature. For an expansion (P₂ < P₁) w<sub>in</sub> comes out negative: work leaves.

blocks.text: Isothermal compression needs the least work and isentropic the most of the reversible paths with 1 < n < γ. A real uncooled compressor is adiabatic but irreversible, and its isentropic efficiency ηc = wisentropic/wactual (typically 0.75 to 0.90) says how much more work it takes. For a turbine the ratio is turned over: ηt = wactual/wisentropic. Several stages with intercooling between them bring a compressor close to the isothermal limit.

Water keeps its density in a pipe; a gas does not, because its pressure and density fall as it speeds up. The Mach number Ma = c/a, with the speed of sound a = √(γRT), decides which effect wins; for air at 300 K, a = √(1.4 × 287 × 300) = 347 m/s. For steady isentropic flow in a duct of area A:

blocks.where: dA and dc are small changes of area and speed along the duct; Ma is the local Mach number.

blocks.text: Below Ma = 1 the flow speeds up only where the duct narrows; above Ma = 1 it speeds up only where the duct widens; Ma = 1 can occur only at the narrowest section, the throat. So a converging nozzle can at most reach sonic speed at its exit, and a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle is needed for supersonic steam or gas jets. The throat pressure at Ma = 1 is the critical pressure: P*/P₀ = [2/(γ + 1)]γ/(γ−1), which is 0.528 for air (γ = 1.4) and about 0.546 for superheated steam (n ≈ 1.3). Once the back pressure falls below P*, the throat stays at Ma = 1 and the mass flow no longer rises: the nozzle is choked.

In a long insulated pipe of constant area, friction lowers the pressure while h + c²/2 stays constant; the density falls, so ṁ = ρAc forces the speed up toward Ma = 1, which the pipe cannot pass. A gas pipeline at Ma well below 0.3 flows close to isothermally.

examples.question: Air enters an adiabatic nozzle at h₁ = 300 kJ/kg and c₁ = 50 m/s, and leaves at h₂ = 280 kJ/kg. Neglect height change. Find the exit speed c₂.
steps: Nozzle: q = 0, w<sub>s</sub> = 0, Δz = 0, so h₁ + c₁²/2 = h₂ + c₂²/2, and c₂²/2 = (h₁ − h₂) + c₁²/2.
Enthalpy drop in J/kg: h₁ − h₂ = 300 − 280 = 20 kJ/kg = 20 000 J/kg = 20 000 m²/s².
Inlet kinetic term: c₁²/2 = 50²/2 = 1250 m²/s² (1.25 kJ/kg).
Check: h₀ = 300 + 1.25 = 280 + 21.25 = 301.25 kJ/kg at both ends.
examples.answer: The exit speed is 206.2 m/s; the stagnation enthalpy stays at 301.25 kJ/kg.

examples.question: An uncooled compressor takes 0.50 kg/s of air at 1.00 bar and 300 K and delivers it at 5.00 bar. Its isentropic efficiency is 0.80. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), γ = 1.4 and R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), and neglect kinetic terms. Find the isentropic exit temperature, the actual work and exit temperature, and the power; compare with reversible isothermal compression.
steps: Isentropic exit: T₂s = 300 × 1.5838 = 475.1 K, and w<sub>isentropic</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₂s − T₁) = 1.005 × 175.1 = 176.0 kJ/kg.
Actual work: w<sub>actual</sub> = w<sub>isentropic</sub>/η<sub>c</sub> = 176.0/0.80 = 220.0 kJ/kg, so T₂ = T₁ + w<sub>actual</sub>/c<sub>p</sub> = 300 + 220.0/1.005 = 518.9 K.
Power: ṁ w<sub>actual</sub> = 0.50 × 220.0 = 110.0 kW (into the air).
Reversible isothermal: w<sub>in</sub> = RT₁ ln 5 = 0.287 × 300 × 1.6094 = 138.6 kJ/kg, power 0.50 × 138.6 = 69.3 kW.
examples.answer: T₂s = 475.1 K; the real machine needs 220.0 kJ/kg, delivers air at 518.9 K and draws 110.0 kW, against 69.3 kW for reversible isothermal compression.

traps: Adding c²/2 in m²/s² straight to h in kJ/kg. Divide the kinetic term by 1000 first: 1 kJ/kg = 1000 m²/s².
Using the closed-system work ∫P dv for a flow compressor. The steady-flow work is ∫v dP; for a polytropic path the two differ by the factor n.
Reversing the compressor sign. In the equation w<sub>s</sub> is work done by the fluid, so for a compressor w<sub>s</sub> = h₁ − h₂ is negative; the work input is h₂ − h₁.
Expecting a converging nozzle to give a supersonic jet. It reaches at most Ma = 1 at its exit; supersonic flow needs a diverging part after the throat.
Using T in °C, or R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), in a = √(γRT); use K and 287 J/(kg·K) for air.

quiz.q: Write the reduced energy equation for a throttling valve and say what stays constant.
quiz.a: h₁ = h₂: with q = 0, w<sub>s</sub> = 0 and negligible kinetic and potential changes, the enthalpy is the same before and after the valve, though the pressure falls.

quiz.q: Why does the temperature of a gas fall as it passes through an insulated nozzle?
quiz.a: No shaft and no heat, so h + c²/2 is constant. The gas gains kinetic energy, which comes out of its own enthalpy; for a gas lower h means lower T.

quiz.q: Air flows at 0.5 kg/s through an adiabatic compressor from h₁ = 290 kJ/kg to h₂ = 350 kJ/kg, with negligible kinetic and height changes. Find the shaft power.
quiz.a: Work input per kg = h₂ − h₁ = 60 kJ/kg; with h in kJ/kg and ṁ in kg/s the product is in kW: 0.5 × 60 = 30 kW supplied to the air (w<sub>s</sub> = −60 kJ/kg).

quiz.q: Air at 250 K moves at 400 m/s. Find the speed of sound and the Mach number.
A converging nozzle draws air from a large tank at 7.0 bar. The back pressure is lowered from 6.0 bar to 2.0 bar. Describe the mass flow.
quiz.a: P* = 0.528 × 7.0 = 3.70 bar. As the back pressure falls from 6.0 to 3.70 bar the exit speed and mass flow rise. Below 3.70 bar the exit is already at Ma = 1, so the nozzle is choked and the mass flow stays constant; the extra expansion happens outside the nozzle.

quiz.q: In the worked compressor example, reversible isothermal compression needs 138.6 kJ/kg and isentropic compression 176.0 kJ/kg. Explain the difference using w<sub>in</sub> = ∫v dP.
quiz.a: Both paths run from 1 to 5 bar, but the isentropic gas heats up to 475 K, so its v at each pressure is larger and the area ∫v dP is larger, by 37.4 kJ/kg. Cooling keeps v small and saves work.

beyond: Not for the exam. Safety-valve and flare design rests on choked flow: once the throat is sonic, only a higher upstream pressure raises the relief rate. Gas dynamics adds shock waves and the Fanno (friction) and Rayleigh (heating) lines. Search for choked flow, de Laval nozzle and compressor polytropic efficiency.
